chunks.content: 96 Why Your Letters of Intent Are Being Ignored Hi Sara, Submitting letters of intent (LOIs) but getting crickets in response? You’re not alone. I’ve talked to hundreds of buyers in the accounting industry, and there’s one big reason LOIs often end up in the seller’s trash bin: you’re not answering the one question sellers care about most. “How Are You Going to Take Care of My Business?” It seems obvious, but for sellers—especially those running CPA firms—it’s the dealbreaker. If your LOI doesn’t explain how you’ll manage their highly regulated and sophisticated practice, especially if you’re not a CPA yourself, you’re unlikely to get a call back. Here’s why: CPA-Specific Work Matters: Not all accounting is created equal. While bookkeeping, payroll, and general tax prep fall under “accounting,” CPA-specific tasks—like audit and attestation work—require that coveted CPA designation. Regulatory Hurdles Exist: In most jurisdictions, CPA firms must be majority-owned by CPAs (51% or more). In some states, like South Carolina, the threshold is even higher at 66.6%. Without a CPA designation, you can’t own these businesses outright. Sellers Care About Their Legacy: Sellers work hard to build their practices. They’re not just selling a business; they’re entrusting their clients to you and sometimes their employees as well. If your plan doesn’t inspire confidence, they’ll pass. How to Fix Your LOI Here’s how to address sellers’ concerns upfront: Have a Clear Ownership Plan: If you’re not a CPA, acknowledge the regulatory requirements and provide a solution that answers their question before they can ask it. Options include: Partnering with a CPA to co-own the firm. Structuring the deal as a general accounting practice (if audit work isn’t involved). Using an alternative practice structure (APS) to spin off CPA-specific tasks into a separate CPA-owned entity. Don’t Default to “I’ll Hire Someone”: Hiring a tax manager or offshoring CPA-specific tasks might sound plenty fine to you, but sellers are understandably very skeptical of this pie in the sky solution. Show you’ve done the homework by (at the very least) identifying or partnering with qualified talent. Even still, you should know that some sellers are simply not going to consider a non-CPA buyer. Prioritize Client Care: Sellers want assurance that their clients will be taken care of. Your LOI should show empathy for their concerns and confidence in your ability to maintain those relationships. At the end of the day, sellers aren’t just chasing the highest offer. They want a buyer who understands the industry, respects their hard work, and has a realistic plan for the future. If you’re struggling to craft LOIs that stand out, check out our Become the Expert: Letter of Intent Course right here.
